newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: ZIMBABWE GOVERNMENT KEEPS TOUGH LINE ON STRIKERS.
newsitem.headline: ZIMBABWE GOVERNMENT KEEPS TOUGH LINE ON STRIKERS.

text.p: Zimbabwe's government on Wednesday maintained its tough stance against striking nurses and doctors while workers continued to ignore union calls for a nationwide industrial stoppage in support of the strikers.

The three-week stoppage by state nurses and doctors has paralysed public hospitals. President Robert Mugabe's government lined up three cabinet ministers at a news conference to reiterate its uncompromising position against them.

"We have given them letters of dismissal which state clearly what they should do," said Industry and Commerce Minister Nathan Shamuyarira who is acting public service, labour and social welfare minister.

This week the government fired 1,000 nurses and 100 doctors. Union officials say 10,000 nurses and 500 doctors are involved in the strike. The government refuses to negotiate over their demands for more pay and better conditions.

Asked when the government expected an end to the crisis, which has led to the closure of the two largest hospitals, Health and Child Welfare Minister Timothy Stamps said: "You have to ask a minister of religion, not a minister of health. I am not a clairvoyant".
Stamps said no expatriates had yet been recruited to replace the strikers as announced last week by Shamuyarira.
Both ministers accused reporters of exaggerating the problems hospitals were facing.
Shamuyarira said he hoped the Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU) would give up its plans for a general strike. He said calls on workers to down tools had "completely flopped".
ZCTU secretary-general Morgan Tsvangirayi told reporters some people outside Harare had heeded the call and the unions would meet on Friday to decide their next step.

"We want government to resolve the crisis in the health sector and as long as the current state remains critical, it is our responsibility to make sure that the situation in the health sector returns to normalcy," he said.

The ZCTU represents about 200,000 of Zimbabwe's two million workers in the key farming, tourism, banking, energy, mining and manufacturing sectors. Its calls are usually heeded by a majority, including the non-unionised workers.

It called a two-day nationwide strike on Monday evening after riot police broke up a planned demonstration organised by the unions, churches and human rights groups to press the government to resolve the health workers' strike.
A majority of Zimbabwe's 180,000 civil servants staged a three-week strike over pay last month.

The government ended that dispute by awarding the workers 20 percent salary rises, and promises of talks on their demands for wage increases of up to 60 percent which the current strikers say it has failed to keep.
